newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST - Run rates seen at center of API views.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Run rates seen at center of API views.

text.p: The American Petroleum Institute's weekly report is expected to show that refinery run rates are again the hingepin affecting this week's supply and demand outlook in the oil complex.
Capacity utilization rates are expected to stay at or slightly below last week's high levels, so production is still seen running high, traders said.

Although steady utilization rates would be modestly favorable for crude demand, they may pressure the gasoline markets from the supply side at a time when seasonal demand has failed to take its annual leading role, they said.
"The runs are at a level (at which) we have been able to absorb just about anything that comes into the United States," said William Brown, president of W.H. Brown & Co.
With refinery runs expected to be firm, traders were having a hard time estimating gasoline's line in the report.

Gasoline consumption leading up to the three-day Memorial Day weekend was expected to have raised demand levels from last week's levels. But with foreign imports of crude still active, and refinery runs largely unabated, the draw on gasoline stocks should be only slight, traders said.

Traders will be looking at the gasoline figures for any sign of the market's seasonal demand. "The concensus is for a gas build, so any draw would be supportive" for the complex, said Al Lindseth at GSC Energy.
Estimates for crude inventories varied significantly, with some traders eyeing draws of up to 3 million barrels while others predicted builds of the same amount.
"The assumption here is that runs will remain roughly the same as last week, with imports remaining slightly higher than last week but nothing that dramatic," Brown said.
"When you run through the arithmetic, I think we ought to have a draw," he said, adding that the estimates "assume flat behaviour" for the western PADDs.

Other traders, however, expected crude stocks to show a build. "A lot of people are expecting crude oil builds, mostly on imports to the Gulf and the East Coast," Lindseth said, "but demand is still good for WTI/Cushing."
"This is typically a crude restocking period. I think the surplus will outweigh refinery needs," he said.
Heating oil stocks were expected to show builds of about 1.6 million barrels on average, with implied demand seen easing from week-ago levels.
